audits.mathematicalReason: First suppose a ≠ b, so f is nonconstant and its iterates have a cofinite domain. Direct composition gives g(z) = [(1+a)z+a(1+b)]/[(1+b)z+a+b^2]. Comparing coefficients in g(g(z)) = z yields either b = −1, when g is the identity, or b^2+2a+1 = 0. In the latter case |a| = 1 gives |b^2+1| = 2. Triangle inequalities then give 1 ≤ |b|^2 ≤ 3. The minimum |b| = 1 is attained at (a,b) = (−1,1), and the maximum √3 at (a,b) = (1,i√3). For the alternative route, distinct fixed points α,β satisfy (f(z)−α)/(f(z)−β) = [(1−α)/(1−β)](z−α)/(z−β); the multiplier must be a nontrivial fourth root of unity, yielding the same two coefficient conditions. A repeated fixed point cannot give a nonidentity finite-order map. Finally, if a = b, the only allowed pair is the vacuous-domain case (−1,−1), which adds only |b| = 1 and changes neither extremum.
limitations: At a = b = −1, f is constant 1 on its domain but f(1) is undefined, so g and g∘g are nowhere defined. The stated domain-qualified identity is vacuously true there; this does not change the answer.

routes.label: Add equations and bound integer gaps

audits.mathematicalReason: Adding the equations gives (a−b)^2+(a−c)^2+(b−c)^2 = 14. Put u = a−b ≥ 0 and v = b−c ≥ 0. Then u^2+uv+v^2 = 7, whose only nonnegative integer solutions are (1,2) and (2,1). Writing c = t, the first case gives a = t+3, b = t+2 and 7t+11 = 2011, which has no integer solution. The second gives a = t+3, b = t+1 and 8t+11 = 2011, so t = 250 and a = 253. This ordered positive triple satisfies both original equations.

An integer root r cannot be zero and determines the rational coefficient k = −5r−12/r. Setting t = |r| gives |k| = 5t+12/t. The strict bound |k| < 200 holds exactly for integer t from 1 through 39, giving 78 possible signed roots. These roots produce distinct coefficients: if one coefficient came from two distinct integer roots, their product would be 12/5 by the roots–coefficients relation, impossible for integers. Hence N = 78.

Using denominator 60, Alex ate 12/60, Beth 20/60, and Cyril 15/60. Dan therefore ate 1−47/60 = 13/60. Since 20 > 15 > 13 > 12, the decreasing order is Beth, Cyril, Dan, Alex. The two assessed scopes directly cover computing the leftover portion and comparing the fractions.

Each original edge retains one middle segment, giving 100 edges of R. Cutting off a vertex of degree d creates a new d-sided face and therefore d additional edges. The total number of these new edges is the sum of the original vertex degrees, which is twice the original edge count: 200. The nonintersecting cuts keep these contributions distinct. Thus R has 100+200 = 300 edges.

Because M and N are positive, cross-multiplication is valid and gives MN = 36. Each positive divisor M determines exactly one positive integer N = 36/M. Since 36 = 2^2·3^2, it has (2+1)(2+1) = 9 positive divisors, giving nine ordered pairs. Listing the divisors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 36 provides the alternative complete enumeration.
